title: T1587.003 — Develop Capabilities - Digital Certificates
subtitle: Watch "Certificate Camouflage": an operator registers a look-alike domain, collects a free certificate, and runs a phishing page.
aria: Animated diagram titled Certificate Camouflage. Seven elements appear: a phishing operator, a domain registrar, a free certificate authority, a public CT log, a phishing server, a victim browser, and a SOC monitor. The animation moves through eight steps, from registering a look-alike domain to blocking the domains and requesting a takedown.

steps.title: Register a look-alike domain
steps.caption: The operator pays a low-cost registrar for a name such as secure-brandc0-login.com . A typosquat is a domain that copies a real name with one or two changed letters, for example a zero instead of an o. The registrar writes the creation date and the owner record into public WHOIS data, the public registry record of who owns a domain. Defender cue: watch new registrations that contain your brand tokens
steps.defender: Source, CI and artifact logs record who changed what and which artifact was published.

steps.title: Request a free certificate
steps.caption: The ACME process starts with a challenge. The CA asks the requester to place a one-time token file on the web server of the domain, then fetches it. Serving the token proves control of the domain. The whole flow is scripted and takes seconds. Defender cue: a short-lived validation record appears in DNS or on the web root. It is easy to miss, but a domain-observation service may catch it

steps.title: Certificate is issued
steps.caption: The CA checks the challenge, signs the certificate, and, by browser policy, writes the record into public CT logs. From this minute, the look-alike domain is visible to anyone who watches the logs, together with its issuer, subject, and validity dates. Defender cue: this is the early-warning moment. A CT watch rule can fire days before the first phishing email

steps.title: SOC checks CT
steps.caption: A CT monitor compares new certificates against brand tokens and look-alike patterns. It scores the match, opens a case, and shows the analyst the certificate fingerprint, issuer, and subject while the phishing site may not even be live yet. Defender cue: automated CT watch can beat the phishing email to the inbox

steps.title: Phishing site starts serving
steps.caption: The operator points the domain at a server that serves a copy of a real login page. The browser shows a padlock, because the certificate is valid and signed by a real CA. Nothing looks wrong to the user. Defender cue: proxy and DNS logs now show the new domain, with certificate fields you have rarely seen before

steps.title: Victim submits credentials
steps.caption: The victim reads the padlock as a trust mark and types a username and password. The browser sends the form to the attacker's server over the encrypted channel the attacker created. Defender cue: egress logs may show the POST to the new domain. Reset exposed credentials quickly

steps.title: Block and take down
steps.caption: The SOC blocks the domains at DNS and proxy level, sends takedown requests to the registrar and the CA, and adds the certificate indicators to threat intelligence so the next campaign is found faster. Defender cue: the domain dies, but the certificate thumbprint, issuer, and subject outlive it. Store all three
